title: Growth Charts: Interpretation and Clinical Application
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Growth charts are essential tools for monitoring a child's physical development over time, identifying deviations from expected growth patterns. They help clinicians diagnose faltering growth, overweight, and stunting, guiding timely interventions. Proper interpretation requires plotting multiple measurements and considering the child's overall clinical picture.

sections.p: Growth charts provide a visual representation of a child's growth parameters (weight, length/height, head circumference, BMI) relative to a reference population. They are crucial for identifying deviations from normal growth, such as faltering growth (also known as failure to thrive), overweight, and stunting. Faltering growth is typically defined as weight persistently below the 3rd centile or a fall across two major centile lines on the growth chart.
b: Plot weight, length/height, head circumference, and BMI (or weight-for-length) on age- and sex-specific charts.
Document date, time, and source of measurements for accuracy.
Recognise faltering growth: weight below 3rd centile or crossing two major centile lines downwards.
Recognise overweight: weight-for-length/BMI above 97th centile or crossing two major centile lines upwards.
Recognise stunting: length/height-for-age below 3rd centile.

sections.p: The severity of growth deviations is assessed by how far the child's measurements fall from the median or expected centile lines. Z-scores provide a more precise statistical measure of deviation than centiles, with -2 to -3 Z-scores indicating moderate and below -3 Z-scores indicating severe deviations.
b: Mild: between 3rd and 10th centile, or Z-score between -1 and -2.
Moderate: below 3rd centile, or Z-score between -2 and -3.
Severe: below 0.4th centile, or Z-score below -3.
Rapid weight gain: crossing two major centile lines upwards, indicating risk of overweight/obesity.

sections.p: Causes of faltering growth are broadly categorised into inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased metabolic demand, and psychosocial factors. In low-resource settings, nutritional deficiencies and infections are paramount.
b: Inadequate caloric intake: poverty, food insecurity, poor feeding practices, maternal depression, neglect.
Chronic infections: HIV, tuberculosis, recurrent malaria, parasitic infections (e.g., schistosomiasis, hookworm).
Malabsorption: persistent diarrhoea, coeliac disease (less common in some regions), cystic fibrosis (rare).
Increased metabolic demand: congenital heart disease, chronic respiratory disease, hyperthyroidism.
Genetic syndromes: Down syndrome, Turner syndrome (often associated with specific growth patterns).
Endocrine disorders: growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism (less common than nutritional causes).

sections.p: Children with growth deviations may present with a range of signs beyond just their growth chart measurements. A thorough history and physical examination are crucial to identify underlying causes.
b: Faltering growth: lethargy, irritability, delayed developmental milestones, recurrent infections, poor skin turgor, muscle wasting.
Overweight/obesity: increased subcutaneous fat, early puberty, joint pain, breathlessness.
Stunting: disproportionately short stature for age, often associated with developmental delays.
Specific signs of underlying conditions: chronic cough (TB), recurrent fever (malaria, HIV), persistent diarrhoea (malabsorption, HIV).

sections.p: Investigations are guided by the history and physical examination findings, aiming to identify the underlying cause of growth deviation. In low-resource settings, prioritise readily available and cost-effective tests.

t.b: Screens for anaemia (iron deficiency common with poor nutrition) and chronic infection (lymphocytosis in HIV, eosinophilia in parasitic infections). — Anaemia suggests nutritional deficiency or chronic disease; abnormal white cell counts can point to infection.

Identifies parasitic infections (e.g., Giardia, Ascaris, hookworm, Schistosoma) or bacterial causes of chronic diarrhoea. — Presence of ova, cysts, or pathogenic bacteria indicates specific infections requiring targeted treatment.

Screens for HIV infection, a common cause of faltering growth and recurrent infections in endemic areas. — Positive result requires confirmation and initiation of antiretroviral therapy and opportunistic infection prophylaxis.

t.a: Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) or GeneXpert MTB/RIF (if available)
t.b: Screens for tuberculosis, a significant cause of chronic illness and weight loss. — Positive TST or detection of MTB DNA indicates TB infection, requiring further evaluation and treatment.
Screens for urinary tract infections, which can cause chronic illness and poor growth. — Pyuria, bacteriuria, or positive culture indicates UTI, requiring antibiotic treatment.

t.a: Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs) (if available and clinically indicated)
t.b: Evaluates for hypothyroidism, a rare but treatable cause of poor growth and developmental delay. — Low T4 and high TSH indicate hypothyroidism, requiring thyroid hormone replacement.
Identifies inadequate caloric or micronutrient intake and assesses the severity of malnutrition. — Inadequate intake or specific deficiencies guide dietary counselling and supplementation.

sections.p: Certain signs and symptoms warrant urgent attention as they may indicate severe underlying pathology or immediate life-threatening complications related to growth failure.
b: Severe acute malnutrition (marasmus or kwashiorkor): requires immediate inpatient nutritional rehabilitation.
Rapidly falling centiles: suggests an acute, severe underlying illness or neglect.
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, lethargy, indicating fluid loss.
Severe developmental delay: may point to neurological impairment or severe chronic illness.
Recurrent severe infections: suggests immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV) or uncontrolled chronic disease.
Hypoglycaemia or hypothermia: common and dangerous complications of severe malnutrition.

sections.p: Management of growth deviations focuses on addressing the underlying cause, providing adequate nutrition, and monitoring progress. A multidisciplinary approach is often necessary.
b: Treat underlying infections: antibiotics for bacterial infections, anti-parasitics for parasitic infections, antiretrovirals for HIV, anti-TB drugs for tuberculosis.
Nutritional rehabilitation: high-energy, nutrient-dense foods; micronutrient supplementation (e.g., Vitamin A, zinc, iron); therapeutic feeding for severe acute malnutrition.
Optimise feeding practices: education for caregivers on appropriate complementary feeding, frequency, and portion sizes.
Address psychosocial factors: counselling for caregivers, referral to social services if neglect or abuse is suspected.
Manage chronic conditions: optimise treatment for congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, or endocrine disorders.
Regular monitoring: frequent growth chart plotting to assess response to interventions.

sections.p: Consistent follow-up is crucial to ensure sustained growth improvement and prevent recurrence of growth problems. Prevention involves promoting optimal infant and young child feeding practices, immunisation, and early detection of health issues.
b: Regular clinic visits: for growth monitoring, nutritional counselling, and developmental assessment.
Immunisation: ensure full vaccination schedule to prevent common childhood infections.
Deworming: regular deworming in endemic areas to prevent parasitic infections.
Vitamin A supplementation: according to national guidelines to reduce morbidity and mortality.
Health education: on hygiene, safe water, and appropriate feeding practices.
Early identification: training community health workers to identify and refer children with growth problems.

sections.p: It's important to differentiate true growth faltering from normal variations in growth or constitutional short stature, which do not require intervention.
b: Constitutional short stature: child is short but growing along a normal centile line, often with short parents and delayed bone age.
Familial short stature: child is short, grows along a normal centile line, and has short parents with normal bone age.
Normal variations in weight gain: temporary dips due to minor illness or changes in feeding, followed by catch-up growth.
Prematurity: growth charts for preterm infants should be adjusted for gestational age until 2 years of age.

sections.p: Growth chart interpretation can be misleading if measurements are inaccurate, plotted incorrectly, or if the child's unique circumstances are not considered. Always verify data and consider the clinical context.
b: Inaccurate measurements: incorrect technique, faulty equipment, or not zeroing scales can lead to false readings.
Incorrect plotting: using the wrong chart (e.g., male chart for female child, or wrong age-range chart) or plotting on the wrong line.
Single measurement: a single point on a growth chart is less informative than a trend over time.
Acute illness: a child may temporarily lose weight during an acute illness, which is not necessarily faltering growth if followed by catch-up.
Ethnicity/genetics: while WHO charts are globally applicable, extreme variations in parental height can influence a child's expected growth trajectory.
Lack of previous data: without prior measurements, it's difficult to assess growth velocity or centile crossing.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling growth centiles across two major lines
Signs of severe dehydration or shock
Persistent vomiting or inability to feed

faq.q: What is the difference between centiles and Z-scores?
faq.a: Centiles indicate the percentage of children in a reference population who are at or below a given measurement. Z-scores are standard deviation units from the median, providing a more precise statistical measure of how far a child's measurement deviates from the average.

faq.q: When should I use weight-for-length versus BMI?
faq.a: Weight-for-length is used for children under 2 years of age to assess proportionality and identify wasting or overweight. BMI (Body Mass Index) is used for children 2 years and older for similar assessments, as length measurement becomes height.

faq.q: Why are head circumference charts important?
faq.a: Head circumference charts monitor brain growth. Deviations (microcephaly or macrocephaly) can indicate underlying neurological issues, such as congenital infections, genetic syndromes, or hydrocephalus, requiring further investigation.

Besides nutritional rehabilitation, what are two critical immediate management steps you would take, and why? — 1. Treat/prevent hypoglycaemia: SAM children have depleted glycogen stores and are prone to low blood sugar. 2. Treat/prevent hypothermia: SAM children have poor thermoregulation due to lack of subcutaneous fat. Both are life-threatening complications.

A mother brings her 18-month-old child, who is consistently on the 3rd centile for length-for-age but on the 50th centile for weight-for-length. What growth problem does this indicate, and what is the most likely long-term consequence if unaddressed? — This indicates stunting (chronic malnutrition). The most likely long-term consequence is impaired cognitive development and reduced adult productivity.

Describe two common errors in plotting growth charts that can lead to misinterpretation, and how to avoid them. — 1. Using the wrong chart (e.g., male chart for a female child, or a chart for a different age range): always verify the child's sex and age against the chart's labels. 2. Plotting a single measurement without considering previous data: always plot multiple points to establish a trend and assess growth velocity; a single point is rarely diagnostic.
